docs.description: "Josef Hofmann Golden Jubilee Concert (Complete) 1. Brahms: Academic Festival Overture (0:20) 2. Introductory remarks by Walter Damrosch (10:04) 3. Rubinstein: Piano Concerto No. 4 in D minor I. Moderato assai - allegro (15:13) II. Andante (27:25) III. Allegro (37:48) Intermission 4. Chopin: Ballade No. 1 in G minor, Op. 23, No. 1 (47:14) 5. Chopin: Nocturne in E-flat, Op.9, No.2 (55:45) 6. Chopin: Waltz in A-flat, Op. 42 (1:00:05) 7. Chopin: Andante Spianato et Grande Polonaise in E-flat, Op. 22 (1:03:50) 8. Chopin: Nocturne in F-sharp, Op. 15, No. 2 (1:15:16) 9. Chopin Waltz in D-flat, Op. 64, No. 1 "Minute" (1:18:16) 10. Chopin: Etude in G-flat, Op. 25, No. 9 "Butterfly" (1:19:53) 11. Chopin Berceuse in B-flat, Op.57 (1:20:59) 12. Hofmann: Chromaticon for Piano and Orchestra (1:24:34) Encores 13. Mendelssohn: Spinning Song in C Major, Op. 67, No. 4 (1:38:59) 14. Rachmaninoff: Prelude in G minor, Op. 23 (1:40:59) 15. Beethoven-Rubinstein: Turkish March (From the Ruins of Athens) (1:44:33) 16. Moszkowski: Caprice Espagnole, Op. 37 (1:46:35) Josef Hofmann, pianist Fritz Reiner, conductor The Curtis Institute Student Orchestra Walter Damrosch, introduction Recorded November 28, 1937 at the Metropolitan Opera House, New York The legendary Gala Concert to mark the 50th Anniversary of Josef Hofmann's first performance in the USA is a landmark in 20th century music. Although we have issued the music from this Gala Concert before as separate pieces, we have never offered it in its entirety. This is the first time the Brahms Overture, this performance of Hofmann's "Chromaticon", and the introduction by Walter Damrosch have been offered on this channel as well. In our prior editions the recordings were kept as close to raw as possible. For the current issue the recording has been optimized a little more with modern sonic technology, and are completely new mixes for this edition. For the present recital Hofmann employed the now archaic practice of extemporizing before selections to get the audience to settle down and prepare to listen. These improvisations are also included here for the first time on this channel. Our aim here is to offer a rare glimpse at the extraordinary pianism of Hofmann, a pianist who shunned recording, with the full dynamic range and tonal quality that was his alone. In spite of modern restoration efforts some artifacts of age and wear are present.
